{{Short description|Function or value which does not change}}
{{for-multi|a narrower treatment related to this subject|Mathematical constant|other meanings of "constant"|Constant (disambiguation)}}
{{CS1 config|mode=cs1}}
In [[mathematics]], the word '''constant''' conveys multiple meanings. As an adjective, it refers to non-variance (i.e. unchanging with respect to some other [[Value (mathematics)|value]]); as a noun, it has two different meanings: 
* A fixed and well-defined [[number]] or other non-changing [[mathematical object]], or the [[Glossary of mathematical symbols|symbol]] denoting it.<ref>{{SpringerEOM|title=Constant|oldid=37036|last=Sobolev|first=S. K.|date=December 20, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{SpringerEOM|title=Individual constant|oldid=55830|last=Sobolev|first=S. K.|date=July 2, 2024}}</ref> The terms ''[[mathematical constant]]'' or ''[[physical constant]]'' are sometimes used to distinguish this meaning.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Definition of CONSTANT|url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/constant|access-date=2021-11-09|website=www.merriam-webster.com|language=en}}</ref>
* A [[Function (mathematics)|function]] whose value remains unchanged (i.e., a ''[[constant function]]'').<ref>{{MathWorld|Constant}}</ref> Such a constant is commonly represented by a [[variable (mathematics)|variable]] which does not depend on the main variable(s) in question.

For example, a general [[quadratic function]] is commonly written as
<math>a x^2 + b x + c</math>,
where {{mvar|a}}, {{mvar|b}}, and {{mvar|c}} are constants ([[coefficient]]s or parameters), and {{mvar|x}} a [[Variable (mathematics)|variable]]—a placeholder for the [[Argument of a function|argument]] of the function being studied. A more explicit way to denote this function is
<math>x\mapsto a x^2 + b x + c</math>,
which makes the function-argument status of {{mvar|x}} (and by extension the constancy of {{mvar|a}}, {{mvar|b}}, and {{mvar|c}}) clear. In this example {{mvar|a}}, {{mvar|b}}, and {{mvar|c}} are coefficients of the [[polynomial]]. Since {{mvar|c}} occurs in a term that does not involve {{mvar|x}}, it is called the [[Constant term|constant term of the polynomial]] and can be thought of as the coefficient of {{math|''x''<sup>0</sup>}}. More generally, any polynomial term or expression of [[Degree of a polynomial|degree]] zero (no variable) is a constant.<ref>{{cite book | last = Foerster | first = Paul A. | title = Algebra and Trigonometry: Functions and Applications, Teacher's Edition | edition = Classics | year = 2006 | isbn = 0-13-165711-9 | publisher = [[Prentice Hall]] | location = Upper Saddle River, NJ | url-access = registration | url = https://archive.org/details/algebratrigonome00paul_0 }}</ref>{{rp|18}}

== Constant function ==
{{Main|Constant function|Nullary}}

A constant may be used to define a [[constant function]] that ignores its arguments and always gives the same value.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Tanton|first=James|title=Encyclopedia of mathematics|date=2005|publisher=Facts on File|isbn=0-8160-5124-0|location=New York|oclc=56057904}}</ref> A constant function of a single variable, such as <math>f(x)=5</math>, has a [[graph of a function|graph]] of a horizontal line parallel to the ''x''-axis.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Algebra|url=https://tutorial.math.lamar.edu/Classes/Alg/Alg.aspx|access-date=2021-11-09|website=tutorial.math.lamar.edu}}</ref> Such a function always takes the same value (in this case 5), because the variable does not appear in the expression defining the function. 
[[File:Graph of a horizontal line.jpg|thumb|Graph of <math>f(x) = 5</math>.|none]]

== Context-dependence ==

The context-dependent nature of the concept of "constant" can be seen in this example from elementary calculus:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dx} 2^x  & = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{2^{x+h} - 2^x} h = \lim_{h\to 0} 2^x\frac{2^h - 1} h \\[8pt]
& = 2^x \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{2^h - 1} h & & \text{since } x \text{ is constant (i.e. does not depend on } h\text{)} \\[8pt]
 & = 2^x \cdot\mathbf{constant,} & & \text{where }\mathbf{constant}\text{ means not depending on } x.
\end{align}</math>
"Constant" means not depending on some variable; not changing as that variable changes. In the first case above, it means not depending on&nbsp;''h''; in the second, it means not depending on&nbsp;''x''. A constant in a narrower context could be regarded as a variable in a broader context.

==Notable mathematical constants==
{{main|List of mathematical constants}}
Some values occur frequently in mathematics and are conventionally denoted by a specific symbol. These standard symbols and their values are called mathematical constants. Examples include:
* 0 ([[zero]]).
* 1 ([[one]]), the [[natural number]] after zero.
* {{pi}} ([[pi]]), the constant representing the [[ratio]] of a circle's circumference to its diameter, approximately equal to 3.142.<ref>{{cite book | last1 = Arndt | first1 = Jörg | last2 = Haenel | first2 = Christoph | title = Pi – Unleashed | url = https://archive.org/details/piunleashed00jarn | url-access = limited | page = [https://archive.org/details/piunleashed00jarn/page/n253 240] | year = 2001 | publisher = Springer | isbn = 978-3540665724}}</ref>
* {{mvar|[[e (mathematical constant)|e]]}}, approximately equal to 2.718.<ref>{{MathWorld|e|title=e}}</ref>
* {{mvar|i}}, the [[imaginary unit]] such that {{math|''i''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} −1}}.<ref>{{MathWorld|i|title=i}}</ref>
* <math alt="Square root of 2">\sqrt{2}</math> ([[square root of 2]]), the length of the diagonal of a square with unit sides, approximately equal to 1.414.<ref>{{MathWorld|PythagorassConstant|title=Pythagoras's Constant}}</ref>
* {{mvar|φ}} ([[golden ratio]]), approximately equal to 1.618, or algebraically, <math>1+ \sqrt{5} \over 2</math>.<ref>{{MathWorld|GoldenRatio|title=Golden Ratio}}</ref>

==Constants in calculus==
{{Unreferenced section|date=November 2025}}
In [[calculus]], constants are treated in several different ways depending on the operation. For example, the [[derivative]] (rate of change) of a constant function is zero. This is because constants, by definition, do not change. Their derivative is hence zero.

Conversely, when [[Antiderivative|integrating]] a constant function, the constant is multiplied by the variable of integration.

During the evaluation of a [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]], a constant remains the same as it was before and after evaluation.

Integration of a function of one variable often involves a [[constant of integration]]. This arises because the [[integral]] is the [[Inverse function|inverse]] (opposite) of the [[derivative]] meaning that the aim of integration is to recover the original function before differentiation. The derivative of a constant function is zero, as noted above, and the differential operator is a linear operator, so functions that only differ by a constant term have the same derivative. To acknowledge this, a constant of integration is added to an [[indefinite integral]]; this ensures that all possible solutions are included. The constant of integration is generally written as 'c', and represents a constant with a fixed but undefined value.

===Examples===
If {{math|''f''}} is the constant function such that <math>f(x) = 72</math> for every {{math|''x''}} then
<math display="block">\begin{align}
           f'(x) &= 0 \\
  \int f(x) \,dx &= 72x + c\\
  \lim_{x\rarr0}f(x)&=72
\end{align}</math>
